screens.title: Lab Orientation & Strategy
screens.narratorSegment: Start every comprehensive lab by reading the entire scenario and requirements carefully. A step-by-step orientation reduces rework and prevents cascading failures. First, identify dependencies between tasks — for example, you must create and format a logical volume and mount it before deploying web content there. Second, sketch your playbook: group tasks by host, decide which modules to use, and list variables like webserver_ip and dbserver_ip. Third, develop incrementally: implement one task, run it, and verify its result on the target node. Fourth, design each task to be idempotent so repeated runs do not alter the intended state. Fifth, set up handlers to reload or restart services only when changes occur; this keeps runs efficient. Sixth, verify and document: run systemctl, df, ls -Zd, curl, and database connectivity tests, and record results for review. A common misconception is to try to write the whole playbook in one pass; that often hides errors and makes debugging difficult. Instead, build, test, and verify in small steps. Now ask yourself: which dependency will you test first and how will you confirm it worked? Lab Orientation & Strategy means read the requirements, plan hosts and modules, build incrementally, enforce idempotence, use handlers, and verify results with manual checks.. In practical terms, a practical six-step approach to solve the multi-node scenario reliably. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › Lab Orientation
Core Claim
A disciplined approach prevents cascading failures: dependencies must be discovered, tasks planned, and verification performed at each step.
Checklist
  • Identify dependencies: volumes, mounts, services, firewall rules.
  • Assign tasks to hosts and choose modules accordingly.
  • Plan handlers for service reloads and restorecon for SELinux.
  • Document verification commands for each requirement.
Common mistake
Rushing through tasks without verifying an earlier step often causes later tasks to fail and obscures the root cause.
Key Takeaway

Small, verified steps with clear dependencies make a multi-node automation task reliable and debuggable.

Practical process (six steps)
1. Read requirements thoroughly
2. Identify dependencies and hosts
3. Sketch playbook structure and vars
4. Implement tasks incrementally
5. Verify state on nodes
6. Document results and reflect
Concrete example
If a task mounts /srv/webapp, test df -h /srv/webapp and ls -Zd /srv/webapp/index.html before configuring SELinux and firewalld rules. Verifying the mount first prevents confusion about missing files or permissions later.

screens.title: Playbook Planning & Host Targeting
screens.narratorSegment: A well-structured playbook reduces mistakes and clarifies ownership of tasks. Begin with one play that targets all hosts and use when: conditions or separate plays for host-specific tasks. Define variables such as webserver_ip and dbserver_ip near the top so modules reference the correct addresses. Use become: yes at the play level to run privileged tasks. Plan handlers for actions like restoring SELinux contexts, reloading firewalld, and restarting services — handlers should be notified only when a change occurs. A concrete example from the template: declare vars webserver_ip and dbserver_ip, then include tasks wrapped in when: inventory_hostname == 'webserver1' and when: inventory_hostname == 'dbserver1' to keep tasks explicit and auditable. A common misconception is to scatter become: yes across many tasks; prefer a single become at the play level for clarity. Finally, prepare a verification checklist you can run manually after the playbook completes. Which host-level checks will prove your playbook succeeded? Plan those checks before you run the first task. Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › Playbook Planning
Claim
A clear variable and host structure prevents mismatched targets and simplifies debugging.
Checklist
  • Declare webserver_ip and dbserver_ip as top-level vars.
  • Use when: inventory_hostname == 'webserver1' for host-specific tasks.
  • Place become: yes at the play level for privileged tasks.
  • Group handlers for SELinux and firewalld reloads.
Misconception
Avoid duplicating variables across tasks; centralize variable definitions to prevent drift and confusion when debugging.
Example play header
---
- name: RHCE Final Practice Lab - WebApp Deployment
  hosts: all
  become: yes
  vars:
    webserver_ip: "192.168.122.10"
    dbserver_ip: "192.168.122.11"
This header centralizes credentials and target IPs so tasks reference variables consistently. Replace placeholder IPs with your lab addresses before running the playbook.
Concrete example
Wrap webserver-only tasks with when: inventory_hostname == 'webserver1' so the playbook remains a single file while tasks execute only where intended.
Key takeaway
A single, well-structured playbook is easier to test and review than many small, ad-hoc scripts: plan first, then implement incrementally.

screens.title: Idempotence, Handlers, and Verification
screens.narratorSegment: Idempotence is the practice of writing tasks that bring a system to a desired state without causing additional changes on subsequent runs. In Ansible, modules are designed to be idempotent when used correctly: the package module installs only if missing, the mount module mounts only if not already mounted, and handlers run only when a change is signaled. A concrete example from the lab is using ansible. posix. sefcontext to register a SELinux file context and a handler that runs restorecon to apply the context only when the sefcontext entry changed. Verification is the complementary step: after the playbook runs, manually confirm outcomes with commands such as systemctl status httpd, df -h /srv/webapp, ls -Zd /srv/webapp/index. html, curl http://localhost/index. html, and mysql client checks from the web server. A common misconception is thinking idempotence eliminates the need for verification; it does not. Idempotence makes reruns safe, but you must still verify that the desired state corresponds to your requirements. End by testing a rerun: if the second run reports no changes for idempotent tasks, that confirms correctness. What manual check will you run first to validate idempotence?

keyIdea.text: Write tasks so re-running the playbook makes no unnecessary changes, and always run manual verification commands to confirm state.

content.html:
Core Concept › Idempotence & Verification
Definition
Idempotence: running a playbook multiple times reaches the same end state without producing unintended changes.
Why it matters
Idempotent playbooks make automation safe to rerun and speed up troubleshooting because they isolate only real changes.
Handler example
- name: Set SELinux context
  ansible.posix.sefcontext:
    target: "/srv/webapp(/.*)?"
    setype: httpd_sys_content_t
    state: present
  notify: Restore SELinux contexts

handlers:
- name: Restore SELinux contexts
  ansible.builtin.command: restorecon -Rv /srv/webapp
Verification checklist
  • systemctl status httpd
  • df -h /srv/webapp
  • ls -Zd /srv/webapp/index.html
  • curl http://localhost/index.html
  • mysql -u webapp_user -p... -h <webserver_ip> webapp_db -e "SELECT 1;"
Common mistake
Skipping verification and assuming idempotence means everything worked. Always confirm with commands on the managed nodes.
Key Takeaway

Idempotence is necessary but not sufficient — pair it with explicit verification steps to prove success.

screens.title: Webserver Tasks: Storage, SELinux, and Service Management
screens.narratorSegment: On webserver1 you will configure several domains: service management, storage, file deployment, SELinux contexts, firewall, and administrative user privileges. Start by ensuring httpd is installed, enabled, and running with the systemd module. Then create an LVM logical volume named webapp_data in vg_app, format it as XFS, create /srv/webapp, and mount it persistently. After the filesystem is present, deploy index. html with the copy module. If files are served from a non-standard path, SELinux will often block access; use ansible. posix. sefcontext to set httpd_sys_content_t for /srv/webapp and a handler to run restorecon so httpd can read the files. Configure firewalld to allow HTTP permanently, and create a webadmin user with a hashed password, then add a sudoers entry granting webadmin the ability to restart httpd without a password. A common pitfall is forgetting the restorecon handler or the correct SELinux type — that causes 403 errors even when httpd and the firewall are correct. Example verification commands include curl to confirm the index. html content and sudo -u webadmin systemctl restart httpd to validate the sudoers line. Which webserver check will you run immediately after the playbook finishes?

keyIdea.text: Install and enable httpd, create and mount webapp_data, deploy content, set SELinux context and handlers, open HTTP in firewalld, and configure webadmin sudo privileges.

content.html:
Process › Webserver Tasks
Core tasks to implement on webserver1
  • Ensure httpd is installed, running, and enabled using ansible.builtin.systemd.
  • Create an LVM logical volume webapp_data (5G) in vg_app and format it with XFS.
  • Create /srv/webapp, mount the LV persistently, and deploy index.html with copy.
  • Set SELinux file contexts with ansible.posix.sefcontext and notify restorecon handler.
  • Open HTTP in firewalld and create webadmin user and sudoers file for restart privileges.
Common mistake
A 403 error after deployment usually indicates SELinux context is missing or restorecon handler did not run. Always include sefcontext and a handler.
Task examples (excerpt)
- name: Ensure httpd is installed, running, and enabled
  ansible.builtin.systemd:
    name: httpd
    state: started
    enabled: yes
  when: inventory_hostname == 'webserver1'

- name: Create webapp_data Logical Volume
  community.general.lvol:
    vg: vg_app
    lv: webapp_data
    size: 5G
    state: present
  when: inventory_hostname == 'webserver1'

- name: Deploy index.html
  ansible.builtin.copy:
    content: "Hello from WebApp!"
    dest: /srv/webapp/index.html
    mode: '0644'
Example verification
curl http://localhost/index.html should return "Hello from WebApp!" and ls -Zd should show httpd_sys_content_t.
Pro tip
Run restorecon -Rv /srv/webapp as a handler after sefcontext changes instead of running it unconditionally to preserve idempotence.
Key Takeaway
Order matters: storage and mount must exist before file deployment, and SELinux contexts must be correct for httpd to serve non-standard paths.

screens.title: Database Tasks & Firewall Restriction
screens.narratorSegment: On dbserver1 the focus is secure database availability for the web server. Ensure mariadb is installed, enabled, and started using the systemd module. Configure firewalld to allow port 3306/tcp in the public zone but limit that rule to webserver1's IP address: this prevents other hosts from connecting while allowing the webapp to function. Use the community. mysql. mysql_db and community. mysql. mysql_user modules to create webapp_db and a user webapp_user with privileges limited to webserver1's IP. A concrete example: set posix. firewalld with port: 3306/tcp and source: webserver_ip so only the web server can reach the database. Verify the setup by attempting a remote mysql connection from webserver1 using the provided credentials; if that fails, inspect firewalld and ensure the source matches the actual webserver IP. A frequent error is forgetting to reload firewalld or using a broad allow rule; always use a source-limited rule and trigger a reload handler. After tasks complete, run mysql -u webapp_user -pwebapp_pass -h webapp_db -e "SELECT 1;" from webserver1 to confirm connectivity. What firewall check will you run first on dbserver1? Database Tasks & Firewall Restriction means install and enable mariadb, create database and limited user, and configure firewalld to allow 3306 only from the web server's ip.. In practical terms, implement mariadb, database creation, and a tight firewall rule on dbserver1. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Install and enable MariaDB, create database and limited user, and configure firewalld to allow 3306 only from the web server's IP.

content.html:
Process › Database Tasks
Essential steps on dbserver1
  • Ensure mariadb is installed, running, and enabled.
  • Create webapp_db using community.mysql.mysql_db.
  • Create webapp_user with password webapp_pass and grant privileges on webapp_db but limit host to webserver_ip.
  • Open 3306/tcp in firewalld only for source webserver_ip and reload the firewall via a handler.
Common mistake
Allowing 3306 globally instead of limiting by source makes the DB accessible to hosts that should not have access and is a security risk.
Task snippet
- name: Ensure mariadb is installed, running, and enabled
  ansible.builtin.systemd:
    name: mariadb
    state: started
    enabled: yes
  when: inventory_hostname == 'dbserver1'

- name: Configure firewalld to allow MariaDB from webserver1
  ansible.posix.firewalld:
    port: 3306/tcp
    permanent: yes
    state: enabled
    zone: public
    source: "{{ webserver_ip }}"
  when: inventory_hostname == 'dbserver1'
Verification
From webserver1: mysql -u webapp_user -pwebapp_pass -h <dbserver_ip> webapp_db -e "SELECT 1;" should succeed.
Pro tip
Test firewall source values with firewall-cmd --list-all on dbserver1 to confirm the rule includes the intended webserver IP.
Key Takeaway
Limit database access by source IP and verify connectivity from the authorized host to prove correct network-level security.

screens.title: Creating Service Users and Safe Sudo Rules
screens.narratorSegment: In a final lab scenario you will often need dedicated service or administrative accounts with precisely scoped privileges. Creating the webadmin user and giving it one narrowly permitted sudo command is a standard requirement. When you create a user with Ansible, prefer the user module and supply a hashed password rather than plain text. This preserves security and mirrors exam expectations. After the account exists, you provide exactly the command it may run without a password by creating a small file under /etc/sudoers. d and validating it with visudo. A common pattern is to allow only a single command such as restarting httpd; that reduces risk compared to granting full passwordless sudo. A typical problem students see is adding a line to /etc/sudoers directly without validate: this can corrupt sudoers and lock out privilege escalation. Another misunderstanding is expecting systemd to accept the sudo change immediately when the file mode or validate fails; always set mode 0440 and use validate: 'visudo -cf %s' to ensure syntactic safety. In an exam-like workflow, build and test this incrementally: create the user, confirm SSH and local login, then deploy the sudoers snippet and run a non-destructive command to verify. Your playbook should include conditional when clauses so tasks only run on the intended host, and handlers are unnecessary here since sudoers changes take effect at file write. Reflect: which parts of your environment need broader access and which need only a single controlled operation?

keyIdea.title: Scoped privilege is safer
keyIdea.text: Create users idempotently, store hashed passwords, and give minimal NOPASSWD sudo rights via validated files in /etc/sudoers.d.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter Final Lab › User & Sudo
Idempotent user creation
Use ansible.builtin.user with hashed passwords to avoid plaintext.
- Always hash a password before placing it in the user task. Ansible supports password_hash filters and vault for secrets.
- Use state: present so repeated runs do not recreate or change unrelated attributes.
Safe sudo rules
Place a validated file in /etc/sudoers.d with mode 0440.
- Use lineinfile or template with validate: 'visudo -cf %s' to avoid locking out sudo.
- Limit commands to the absolute executable path for predictability.
Key Takeaway

Make user tasks repeatable and validate any sudoer content. Scoped NOPASSWD entries are exam-friendly and safer than broad sudo access.

Example playbook tasks
Code snippet
- name: Create webadmin user on webserver1
  ansible.builtin.user:
    name: webadmin
    password: "{{ 'redhat' | password_hash('sha512') }}"
    state: present
  when: inventory_hostname == 'webserver1'

- name: Allow webadmin to restart httpd without password on webserver1
  ansible.builtin.lineinfile:
    path: /etc/sudoers.d/webadmin_sudo
    create: yes
    mode: '0440'
    line: 'webadmin ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl restart httpd'
    validate: 'visudo -cf %s'
  when: inventory_hostname == 'webserver1'
Scenario
Confirm webadmin can restart httpd without password by running the sudo command as that user in verification steps.
Common mistake
Putting raw sudoers content without validate or wrong file mode can make sudo unusable; use validate and mode 0440.

screens.title: Reliable LVM Creation and Filesystem Idempotency
screens.narratorSegment: Managing block devices and logical volumes in an automated exam-style lab demands careful, idempotent steps. The goal is to create an LV called webapp_data if it doesn't exist, format it with XFS, and mount it persistently at /srv/webapp. Start by verifying the physical volume and volume group exist; if vg_app is absent in your environment you must create the PV and VG first, but in most exam tasks it is provided or simulated. Use community. general. lvol with state: present to create the logical volume idempotently. The filesystem module will only format the device if it lacks the requested fs type, which preserves data if the LV already exists. For mounting, ansible. posix. mount with state: mounted and persistent options will ensure /etc/fstab entries are correct and the mount survives reboots. Common pitfalls include formatting the wrong device due to hard-coded paths and assuming device names are consistent; prefer /dev/vg_app/webapp_data when creating and verifying. Another common mistake is not waiting for kernel recognition of the new device; tasks may need a short delay or a handler to refresh udev in some environments. After each step run verification commands like df -h and lsblk on the managed node. Always test these tasks with --check to preview changes and use a sequential approach: create LV, format, create mount point, mount. That incremental workflow reduces cascading failures and makes debugging much easier. Which verification command will you run first after creating the LV?

keyIdea.title: Make storage tasks defensive
keyIdea.text: Create LVs and filesystems idempotently, verify device paths, and mount persistently so repeated runs are safe.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter Final Lab › LVM & Filesystem
Process: idempotent storage tasks
  1. Confirm vg_app exists or create PV & VG if required.
  2. Create logical volume webapp_data with community.general.lvol (state: present).
  3. Format with ansible.builtin.filesystem only if needed (fstype: xfs).
  4. Create mount directory and mount with ansible.posix.mount (state: mounted, opts: defaults).
  5. Verify with lsblk, df -h, and mount output; add handlers if restore or reload is needed.
Idempotence checklist
  • Use state: present for LVs.
  • Avoid formatting an already formatted device.
  • Persist mounts via fstab through mount module.
Pro Tip

If you're uncertain whether an LV was created previously, run a quick lsblk or vgdisplay in a debug task before formatting.

Playbook excerpt
Mount & Format
# Create LV (idempotent)
- name: Create webapp_data Logical Volume on webserver1
  community.general.lvol:
    vg: vg_app
    lv: webapp_data
    size: 5G
    state: present
  when: inventory_hostname == 'webserver1'

# Format only if needed
- name: Format webapp_data LV with XFS on webserver1
  ansible.builtin.filesystem:
    fstype: xfs
    dev: "/dev/vg_app/webapp_data"
  when: inventory_hostname == 'webserver1'

# Mount persistently
- name: Mount webapp_data LV persistently on webserver1
  ansible.posix.mount:
    path: /srv/webapp
    src: "/dev/vg_app/webapp_data"
    fstype: xfs
    state: mounted
    opts: defaults
  when: inventory_hostname == 'webserver1'
Verify
Run df -h /srv/webapp and lsblk to confirm the LV and mount are correct.
Avoid
Do not blindly format a device path without confirming it belongs to your LV. That risks data loss.

screens.title: SELinux Contexts for Web Content
screens.narratorSegment: SELinux is frequently the silent blocker when web content is unreachable despite running services and open firewall ports. In the lab scenario, you will deploy content to /srv/webapp, which is a non-standard path for Apache. To allow httpd to serve those files you must set the appropriate SELinux file context and ensure the kernel label store is updated. Use ansible. posix. sefcontext to declare the context pattern, for example setting httpd_sys_content_t for /srv/webapp(/.*)?. After changing or adding a sefcontext entry, you must run restorecon to apply labels; in the provided playbook we trigger restorecon via a handler. A common misconception is that setting file modes alone is sufficient; SELinux can still block access even if permissions are correct. Another trap is forgetting to use the correct regex pattern when targeting directories recursively — the typical pattern includes '(/.*)?' to cover nested files. When testing, ls -Zd /srv/webapp/index. html will show the SELinux type; if it is not httpd_sys_content_t, httpd will be denied. If you get a 403 despite correct httpd and firewall settings, SELinux is the leading candidate. For exam conditions, document your sefcontext lines in comments and include a handler that runs restorecon -Rv on the directory. This keeps your playbook explicit about intent and ensures consistent labels after subsequent deployments. As a quick sanity check, temporarily setting SELinux to permissive during debugging can confirm whether SELinux is the blocker, but always restore enforcing mode and then fix contexts rather than leaving permissive in place.

keyIdea.text: Define sefcontext entries and run restorecon so httpd can read files under non-standard directories like /srv/webapp.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter Final Lab › SELinux Contexts
Define and apply file contexts
- name: Set correct SELinux context for /srv/webapp on webserver1
  ansible.posix.sefcontext:
    target: "/srv/webapp(/.*)?"
    setype: httpd_sys_content_t
    state: present
  when: inventory_hostname == 'webserver1'
  notify: Restore SELinux contexts on webserver1

# Handler (defined under handlers)
- name: Restore SELinux contexts on webserver1
  ansible.builtin.command: restorecon -Rv /srv/webapp
  when: inventory_hostname == 'webserver1'
- After applying sefcontext, always run restorecon to update on-disk labels.
- Verify with: ls -Zd /srv/webapp/index.html to confirm the type is httpd_sys_content_t.
Common pitfall

A 403 Forbidden despite running httpd and opening firewalld mostly indicates SELinux prevents file access. Fix contexts, don't disable SELinux in production.

Quick checks
  • ls -Zd <file>
  • restorecon -Rv <dir>
  • audit2allow review when denials exist
Why it matters
SELinux enforces mandatory access control. Correct contexts allow services to safely access resources without loosening global policies.

screens.title: Scoping firewalld rules by service vs. source
screens.narratorSegment: Network controls are a core defense in the exam lab. The requirement to allow MariaDB only from webserver1's IP is a concrete example of scoping firewall rules. Firewalld supports enabling a named service like http widely, but database access should be limited by source. The playbook uses ansible. posix. firewalld with port: 3306/tcp and source: the webserver IP to allow connections only from that address. Contrast two common approaches: enabling the MariaDB service globally versus enabling a port with a source restriction. Allowing the service globally opens the database to the network and increases attack surface. Using a source-limited rule permits only the control host you declare and improves security posture. Another frequent student error is forgetting to reload or reconfigure the zone so the new rule takes effect; use the handler that reloads firewalld after changes. Also document which zone you modify — many exams assume the public zone; changing the wrong zone silently leaves access blocked. Test connectivity from webserver1 using the mysql client to ensure the rule works and that the service listens on the correct interface. If a connection still fails even though the rule looks right, verify SELinux contexts, bind addresses in the database configuration, and DNS name resolution. In short, prefer precise, source-scoped firewall entries for inter-node services and keep broad service openings to a minimum.

keyIdea.text: Allow database ports only from the web server's IP; avoid enabling broad service access when not required.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter Final Lab › Firewall Scoping
A: Enable service globally
Less secure
Enabling the MariaDB service opens port 3306 across the zone. This is simple but allows any host in the zone to attempt connections. Use only when broad access is intended.
B: Allow port with source restriction
Recommended for DB
Using source: "{{ webserver_ip }}" restricts access to only the web server. This reduces attack surface and matches the lab requirement to permit only webserver1.
Playbook excerpt
- name: Configure firewalld to allow MariaDB from webserver1 on dbserver1
  ansible.posix.firewalld:
    port: 3306/tcp
    permanent: yes
    state: enabled
    zone: public
    source: "{{ webserver_ip }}"
  when: inventory_hostname == 'dbserver1'
  notify: Reload firewalld on dbserver1

# Verification from control node:
# mysql -u webapp_user -pwebapp_pass -h 192.168.122.11 webapp_db -e "SELECT 1;"
Test
Test connectivity from webserver1's IP with the mysql client to validate the rule.
Troubleshoot
If blocked, check zone, source syntax, and that firewalld was reloaded by the handler.

screens.title: Verify, Test, and Debug the Full Playbook
screens.narratorSegment: Verification is the final and essential phase of any comprehensive lab. Before you run a large playbook against many nodes, use ansible-playbook --syntax-check to catch YAML or Jinja issues and ansible-playbook --check to preview changes. These commands will not replace careful manual verification on target hosts. After the playbook runs, the lab requires manual checks: systemctl status httpd and mariadb, df -h for the mounted filesystem, ls -Zd to confirm SELinux labels, curl to fetch the index page, and a remote mysql client test to validate DB connectivity. If any test fails, adopt a methodical approach: review the task output to find the first failed task, check handlers that may have been skipped, then SSH into the affected node and run the recommended manual commands to see real-time system state. A frequent error is rushing; if an earlier step fails silently and you proceed, later tasks often cascade into confusing failures. Use small, focused runs targeting a single host with -l to reproduce and debug. Document each fix you apply; the post-lab review should capture what failed and why, so you know which areas need more practice. If firewall or SELinux issues persist, isolate network checks with ping and ss -ltn, check firewalld --list-all, and consult audit logs for SELinux denials. Finally, reflect on idempotence by re-running the playbook and confirming there are no unwanted changes; this confirms your tasks are safe to repeat. What single verification command will you make your habit after every successful run?

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter Final Lab › Verification
Command checklist
  • ansible-playbook rhce_final_lab.yml --syntax-check
  • ansible-playbook rhce_final_lab.yml --check
  • SSH to webserver1: systemctl status httpd, df -h /srv/webapp, ls -Zd /srv/webapp/index.html, curl http://localhost/index.html
  • SSH to dbserver1: systemctl status mariadb, firewall-cmd --list-all, mysql -u webapp_user -pwebapp_pass -h <webserver_ip> webapp_db -e "SELECT 1;"
Debug flow
  1. Find the first failing task in playbook output.
  2. Run the equivalent manual command on the host to observe real errors.
  3. Fix the root cause, document it, and re-run the targeted playbook section.
Example verification outputs

Hello from WebApp!

-rw-r--r--. root root unconfined_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t:s0 /srv/webapp/index.html

| 1 |

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: This final review highlights the core ideas you must retain. First, idempotence: design playbooks so running them repeatedly leaves systems in the desired state and avoids destructive side effects. This relies on choosing the right modules and state settings. Second, scoped security: limit firewall access and sudo privileges to just what is needed, and use SELinux file contexts to permit services to access non-standard directories. Third, verification and incremental testing: use syntax-check and check modes, test tasks on single hosts, and run manual verification commands to confirm outcomes. A common exam trap is rushing through tasks without validating intermediate states; that often produces cascading failures that are hard to debug. Keep concise documentation in your playbook, use handlers for service reloads only when changes occur, and prefer small, testable commits rather than large sweeping runs. Practice the lab workflow until planning, incremental development, verification, and post-lab review become habits. That discipline is what separates a passing automation script from a reliable, production-ready playbook. Which single routine will you adopt to make your playbooks safer and easier to troubleshoot?

fullNarratorScript:
This final lab ties together the Ansible skills and RHEL system administration practices you learned throughout the course. You will plan and implement a single playbook that configures a web server on webserver1 and a database on dbserver1, including service management, logical volume creation, SELinux contexts, firewall rules, user and sudo setup, and database user/database creation. The exercise is deliberately multi-step so you practice designing idempotent tasks, using handlers, and verifying state on managed nodes. A practical habit to adopt is incremental development: implement and test each task before advancing, and use ansible-playbook --check and --syntax-check to catch issues early. In this lab you will also practice targeted firewall rules that limit access by IP and use community and builtin Ansible modules appropriate for each domain. When you complete the lab, perform the verification steps outlined: service status checks, filesystem and SELinux checks, HTTP content retrieval, and database connectivity from the web server. That verification is as important as writing the playbook because it confirms idempotence and reveals integration issues. As you work, ask: what failed and why, and how does one change affect the next step?

These learning objectives focus on applied automation and verification. First, you'll apply accumulated Ansible skills to design and implement a comprehensive playbook that solves an interconnected administration scenario, which matters because integration is where individual tasks become reliable systems. Second, you'll integrate troubleshooting and optimization practices into automation — for example, using ansible-playbook --check to validate changes before applying them and using handlers to reduce unnecessary service restarts. Start every comprehensive lab by reading the entire scenario and requirements carefully. A step-by-step orientation reduces rework and prevents cascading failures. First, identify dependencies between tasks — for example, you must create and format a logical volume and mount it before deploying web content there. Second, sketch your playbook: group tasks by host, decide which modules to use, and list variables like webserver_ip and dbserver_ip. Third, develop incrementally: implement one task, run it, and verify its result on the target node. Fourth, design each task to be idempotent so repeated runs do not alter the intended state. Fifth, set up handlers to reload or restart services only when changes occur; this keeps runs efficient. Sixth, verify and document: run systemctl, df, ls -Zd, curl, and database connectivity tests, and record results for review. A common misconception is to try to write the whole playbook in one pass; that often hides errors and makes debugging difficult. Instead, build, test, and verify in small steps. Now ask yourself: which dependency will you test first and how will you confirm it worked? Idempotence is the practice of writing tasks that bring a system to a desired state without causing additional changes on subsequent runs. In Ansible, modules are designed to be idempotent when used correctly: the package module installs only if missing, the mount module mounts only if not already mounted, and handlers run only when a change is signaled. A concrete example from the lab is using ansible. posix. sefcontext to register a SELinux file context and a handler that runs restorecon to apply the context only when the sefcontext entry changed. Verification is the complementary step: after the playbook runs, manually confirm outcomes with commands such as systemctl status httpd, df -h /srv/webapp, ls -Zd /srv/webapp/index. html, curl http://localhost/index. html, and mysql client checks from the web server. A common misconception is thinking idempotence eliminates the need for verification; it does not. Idempotence makes reruns safe, but you must still verify that the desired state corresponds to your requirements. End by testing a rerun: if the second run reports no changes for idempotent tasks, that confirms correctness. What manual check will you run first to validate idempotence?

On webserver1 you will configure several domains: service management, storage, file deployment, SELinux contexts, firewall, and administrative user privileges. Start by ensuring httpd is installed, enabled, and running with the systemd module. Then create an LVM logical volume named webapp_data in vg_app, format it as XFS, create /srv/webapp, and mount it persistently. After the filesystem is present, deploy index. html with the copy module. If files are served from a non-standard path, SELinux will often block access; use ansible. posix. sefcontext to set httpd_sys_content_t for /srv/webapp and a handler to run restorecon so httpd can read the files. Configure firewalld to allow HTTP permanently, and create a webadmin user with a hashed password, then add a sudoers entry granting webadmin the ability to restart httpd without a password. A common pitfall is forgetting the restorecon handler or the correct SELinux type — that causes 403 errors even when httpd and the firewall are correct. Example verification commands include curl to confirm the index. html content and sudo -u webadmin systemctl restart httpd to validate the sudoers line. Which webserver check will you run immediately after the playbook finishes?

On dbserver1 the focus is secure database availability for the web server. Ensure mariadb is installed, enabled, and started using the systemd module. Configure firewalld to allow port 3306/tcp in the public zone but limit that rule to webserver1's IP address: this prevents other hosts from connecting while allowing the webapp to function. Use the community. mysql. mysql_db and community. mysql. mysql_user modules to create webapp_db and a user webapp_user with privileges limited to webserver1's IP. A concrete example: set posix. firewalld with port: 3306/tcp and source: webserver_ip so only the web server can reach the database. Verify the setup by attempting a remote mysql connection from webserver1 using the provided credentials; if that fails, inspect firewalld and ensure the source matches the actual webserver IP. A frequent error is forgetting to reload firewalld or using a broad allow rule; always use a source-limited rule and trigger a reload handler. After tasks complete, run mysql -u webapp_user -pwebapp_pass -h webapp_db -e "SELECT 1;" from webserver1 to confirm connectivity. What firewall check will you run first on dbserver1? In a final lab scenario you will often need dedicated service or administrative accounts with precisely scoped privileges. Creating the webadmin user and giving it one narrowly permitted sudo command is a standard requirement. When you create a user with Ansible, prefer the user module and supply a hashed password rather than plain text. This preserves security and mirrors exam expectations. After the account exists, you provide exactly the command it may run without a password by creating a small file under /etc/sudoers. d and validating it with visudo. A common pattern is to allow only a single command such as restarting httpd; that reduces risk compared to granting full passwordless sudo. A typical problem students see is adding a line to /etc/sudoers directly without validate: this can corrupt sudoers and lock out privilege escalation. Another misunderstanding is expecting systemd to accept the sudo change immediately when the file mode or validate fails; always set mode 0440 and use validate: 'visudo -cf %s' to ensure syntactic safety. In an exam-like workflow, build and test this incrementally: create the user, confirm SSH and local login, then deploy the sudoers snippet and run a non-destructive command to verify. Your playbook should include conditional when clauses so tasks only run on the intended host, and handlers are unnecessary here since sudoers changes take effect at file write. Reflect: which parts of your environment need broader access and which need only a single controlled operation?

Managing block devices and logical volumes in an automated exam-style lab demands careful, idempotent steps. The goal is to create an LV called webapp_data if it doesn't exist, format it with XFS, and mount it persistently at /srv/webapp. Start by verifying the physical volume and volume group exist; if vg_app is absent in your environment you must create the PV and VG first, but in most exam tasks it is provided or simulated. Use community. general. lvol with state: present to create the logical volume idempotently. The filesystem module will only format the device if it lacks the requested fs type, which preserves data if the LV already exists. For mounting, ansible. posix. mount with state: mounted and persistent options will ensure /etc/fstab entries are correct and the mount survives reboots. Common pitfalls include formatting the wrong device due to hard-coded paths and assuming device names are consistent; prefer /dev/vg_app/webapp_data when creating and verifying. Another common mistake is not waiting for kernel recognition of the new device; tasks may need a short delay or a handler to refresh udev in some environments. After each step run verification commands like df -h and lsblk on the managed node. Always test these tasks with --check to preview changes and use a sequential approach: create LV, format, create mount point, mount. That incremental workflow reduces cascading failures and makes debugging much easier. Which verification command will you run first after creating the LV?

SELinux is frequently the silent blocker when web content is unreachable despite running services and open firewall ports. In the lab scenario, you will deploy content to /srv/webapp, which is a non-standard path for Apache. To allow httpd to serve those files you must set the appropriate SELinux file context and ensure the kernel label store is updated. Use ansible. posix. sefcontext to declare the context pattern, for example setting httpd_sys_content_t for /srv/webapp(/.*)?. After changing or adding a sefcontext entry, you must run restorecon to apply labels; in the provided playbook we trigger restorecon via a handler. A common misconception is that setting file modes alone is sufficient; SELinux can still block access even if permissions are correct. Another trap is forgetting to use the correct regex pattern when targeting directories recursively — the typical pattern includes '(/.*)?' to cover nested files. When testing, ls -Zd /srv/webapp/index. html will show the SELinux type; if it is not httpd_sys_content_t, httpd will be denied. If you get a 403 despite correct httpd and firewall settings, SELinux is the leading candidate. For exam conditions, document your sefcontext lines in comments and include a handler that runs restorecon -Rv on the directory. This keeps your playbook explicit about intent and ensures consistent labels after subsequent deployments. As a quick sanity check, temporarily setting SELinux to permissive during debugging can confirm whether SELinux is the blocker, but always restore enforcing mode and then fix contexts rather than leaving permissive in place.

Network controls are a core defense in the exam lab. The requirement to allow MariaDB only from webserver1's IP is a concrete example of scoping firewall rules. Firewalld supports enabling a named service like http widely, but database access should be limited by source. The playbook uses ansible. posix. firewalld with port: 3306/tcp and source: the webserver IP to allow connections only from that address. Contrast two common approaches: enabling the MariaDB service globally versus enabling a port with a source restriction. Allowing the service globally opens the database to the network and increases attack surface. Using a source-limited rule permits only the control host you declare and improves security posture. Another frequent student error is forgetting to reload or reconfigure the zone so the new rule takes effect; use the handler that reloads firewalld after changes. Also document which zone you modify — many exams assume the public zone; changing the wrong zone silently leaves access blocked. Test connectivity from webserver1 using the mysql client to ensure the rule works and that the service listens on the correct interface. If a connection still fails even though the rule looks right, verify SELinux contexts, bind addresses in the database configuration, and DNS name resolution. In short, prefer precise, source-scoped firewall entries for inter-node services and keep broad service openings to a minimum.

Verification is the final and essential phase of any comprehensive lab. Before you run a large playbook against many nodes, use ansible-playbook --syntax-check to catch YAML or Jinja issues and ansible-playbook --check to preview changes. These commands will not replace careful manual verification on target hosts. After the playbook runs, the lab requires manual checks: systemctl status httpd and mariadb, df -h for the mounted filesystem, ls -Zd to confirm SELinux labels, curl to fetch the index page, and a remote mysql client test to validate DB connectivity. If any test fails, adopt a methodical approach: review the task output to find the first failed task, check handlers that may have been skipped, then SSH into the affected node and run the recommended manual commands to see real-time system state. A frequent error is rushing; if an earlier step fails silently and you proceed, later tasks often cascade into confusing failures. Use small, focused runs targeting a single host with -l to reproduce and debug. Document each fix you apply; the post-lab review should capture what failed and why, so you know which areas need more practice. If firewall or SELinux issues persist, isolate network checks with ping and ss -ltn, check firewalld --list-all, and consult audit logs for SELinux denials. Finally, reflect on idempotence by re-running the playbook and confirming there are no unwanted changes; this confirms your tasks are safe to repeat. This final review highlights the core ideas you must retain. First, idempotence: design playbooks so running them repeatedly leaves systems in the desired state and avoids destructive side effects. This relies on choosing the right modules and state settings. Second, scoped security: limit firewall access and sudo privileges to just what is needed, and use SELinux file contexts to permit services to access non-standard directories. Third, verification and incremental testing: use syntax-check and check modes, test tasks on single hosts, and run manual verification commands to confirm outcomes. A common exam trap is rushing through tasks without validating intermediate states; that often produces cascading failures that are hard to debug. Keep concise documentation in your playbook, use handlers for service reloads only when changes occur, and prefer small, testable commits rather than large sweeping runs. Practice the lab workflow until planning, incremental development, verification, and post-lab review become habits. That discipline is what separates a passing automation script from a reliable, production-ready playbook. Which single routine will you adopt to make your playbooks safer and easier to troubleshoot?

Second, build and test incrementally — add one task at a time and verify it behaves idempotently. Third, document key choices and include comments in your playbook so reviewers and you later understand the rationale. Finally, after completion, perform a structured post-lab review: list successes, note failures, and convert problems into practice items. Doing this not only prepares you for the RHCE exam but also builds professional habits you will use in real operations. Keep a short checklist of verification commands and use it every run — it saves time and prevents avoidable mistakes.
